name: Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm

matching.reasoningTemplate: Back/abdominal pain with hypotension in an older patient is a ruptured AAA until proven otherwise.

redFlags: Hypotension + back pain + pulsatile mass = surgical emergency

clinicalPearls: Most abdominal aortic aneurysms are asymptomatic and are found as an incidental imaging finding or as a palpable, pulsatile, expansile, nontender mass on routine abdominal exam (p.2211).
New aneurysmal pain is usually a harbinger of rupture and constitutes a medical emergency; however, acute rupture more often occurs without any prior warning (p.2211).
Acute pain plus hypotension is the presentation of frank rupture and mandates emergency open or endovascular repair (p.2211).
At least 90% of abdominal aortic aneurysms >4.0 cm are atherosclerotic, and most lie below the level of the renal arteries (infrarenal) (p.2211).
Cigarette smoking is the most potent modifiable risk factor; incidence rises with age and the condition is more common in men (p.2211).
Mural thrombus within the aneurysm sac can be a source of peripheral (distal) embolization (p.2211).
harrison.pathophysiology: Aneurysm is a pathologic dilation of the aortic wall; a true aneurysm involves all three wall layers, versus a pseudoaneurysm in which intima and media are disrupted and the dilated segment is contained only by adventitia (and sometimes perivascular clot). Most abdominal aortic aneurysms are degenerative and atherosclerotic. Wall failure results from degradation or abnormal production of the structural matrix proteins elastin and collagen, driven by inflammation, oxidative stress, proteolysis, and biomechanical wall stress. B- and T-lymphocytes, macrophages, inflammatory cytokines, and matrix metalloproteinases degrade elastin and collagen, reducing tensile strength and the aorta's ability to tolerate pulsatile stretch; histology shows elastin/collagen destruction, loss of vascular smooth muscle, neovascularization, and inflammation (p.2208).
additionalDifferentials: Acute mesenteric ischemia (SMA embolism/thrombosis) — also causes severe diffuse abdominal pain, classically pain out of proportion to exam findings (p.154).
Thoracic / thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm, which is often contiguous with infradiaphragmatic disease (p.2208).
infectionMimics: Mycotic (infective) aortic aneurysm from staphylococcal, streptococcal, Salmonella, or fungal seeding — typically saccular and often with positive blood cultures (p.2209).
Syphilitic aortitis — uncommon cause, predominantly involves the ascending aorta/arch rather than the abdominal aorta (p.2209).
Tuberculous aneurysm — typically affects the thoracic aorta via contiguous spread from hilar nodes or abscess (p.2209).
nonInfectiousMimics: Renal/ureteric colic — rupturing AAA pain radiating to flank or genitalia can mimic urolithiasis (p.154).
Rectus sheath hematoma — abdominal wall mass and pain, especially on anticoagulants (p.154).
additionalInvestigations: Abdominal ultrasound — delineates transverse and longitudinal dimensions, can detect mural thrombus, and is the tool for serial size surveillance and screening (p.2211).
Plain abdominal radiograph — may show a calcified aneurysm outline, but ~25% are non-calcified and not visualized (p.2211).
Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI — accurate for location and size and for planning open or endovascular repair (p.2211).
Contrast aortography may underestimate true diameter when mural thrombus reduces luminal size, and carries risks of bleeding, allergy, and atheroembolism (p.2211).
redFlags: New or worsening aneurysmal pain (abdomen, lower back, chest, or scrotum) signals impending rupture (p.2211).
Abdominal pain radiating to sacrum, flank, or genitalia should always raise suspicion of a rupturing AAA (p.154).
Acute pain with hypotension indicates rupture — emergency repair required (p.2211).
harrison.prognosis: Prognosis depends on aneurysm size and on the severity of coexisting coronary and cerebrovascular disease. Rupture risk rises sharply with diameter: the 5-year rupture risk is roughly 1-2% for aneurysms <5 cm versus 20-40% for aneurysms >5 cm. At smaller diameters the rupture risk is higher in women than in men (p.2211-2212).
pitfalls: A rupturing AAA can be misattributed to renal/ureteric colic when pain radiates to the flank or genitalia (p.154).
Plain x-ray cannot exclude an aneurysm because roughly a quarter are non-calcified (p.2211).
Aortography may underestimate aneurysm diameter when mural thrombus narrows the lumen (p.2211).
Premonitory pain may persist for several days before rupture and collapse, so an evolving symptomatic aneurysm should not be dismissed (p.154).
harrison.severityClassification: Rupture-risk stratification is driven by maximal aortic diameter. Per Harrison: a true abdominal aortic aneurysm is dilation 50% greater than the adjacent normal segment; aneurysms >=4.0 cm affect 1-2% of men >50. 5-year rupture risk is ~1-2% for <5 cm and ~20-40% for >5 cm. Repair thresholds: any size if rapidly expanding or symptomatic; for asymptomatic aneurysms repair is indicated at >=5.5 cm in men and >=5.0 cm in women, with smaller aneurysms followed by ultrasound surveillance (p.2210-2212).
